MultipleChoice.prompt: A developer has an inherent function `Config::parse_from(s: &str) -> Result<Config, ParseError>` and wants the CLI to write `arg.parse::<Config>()`. What is the right way to make this work, and why?
options: Add an inherent method named `parse` on the type; `str::parse` automatically finds methods with that name on the target type.
Implement `From<&str>` for the type; `str::parse` falls back to `From` and converts any parse error into a panic.
Make the existing parse function return `Result<T, String>`; any function with that signature is picked up by `str::parse`.
Implement `FromStr` for the type, with an associated `Err` type for failures, so that `str::parse::<T>()` can call `T::from_str`.

questions.explanation: `str::parse::<T>()` is bounded on `T: FromStr` and simply calls `T::from_str`, so implementing the trait is what makes `.parse()` compile for the type. Having an inherent function with a similar name or an `Err` type that implements `Display` does not satisfy the trait bound, and `From<&str>` is for infallible conversions and is not what `parse` uses.

MultipleChoice.prompt: A CLI handler contains `let parsed = input.parse()?;` and the compiler reports "type annotations needed". The author fixes it with `let parsed: Identity = input.parse()?;`, and uses `input.parse::<Identity>()` in tests. Why was the annotation (or turbofish) required?
options: The compiler inspects the string literal at compile time and picks the type that fits its contents, so the annotation is only documentation.
The annotation makes `parse()` return a `Result`; without it `parse()` would return the value directly and panic on invalid input.
The return type of `parse()` is generic and nothing else in the expression determines it, so the compiler cannot choose which `FromStr` implementation to use without an annotation or turbofish.
Without it, `parse()` defaults to returning `String`, which would silently produce the wrong type at runtime.

questions.explanation: `str::parse<F>` is generic over its return type F, and nothing in `let parsed = s.parse()?;` tells the compiler which type to produce. An annotation on the binding or a turbofish supplies F, and the right `FromStr` implementation is then chosen. The tempting idea that the type is inferred from the string contents is wrong, because inference happens at compile time from types only.

MultipleChoice.prompt: A function returns `Result<T, String>` and calls an operation that returns `Result<U, std::num::ParseIntError>`. The author writes `let n = s.parse::<i32>().map_err(|e: std::num::ParseIntError| e.to_string())?;`. Why is the `map_err` call needed here?
options: `?` only converts errors using `From`, and there is no `From` impl from most error types into `String`, so `map_err` must convert the error to a `String` first or the code will not compile.
`map_err` converts the `Ok` value to a `String` so that `?` can unwrap it and return it from the function.
`map_err` is needed because `?` cannot be used on a `Result` unless its error type is already `String`; otherwise it panics at runtime.
`?` automatically calls `to_string()` on any error that implements `Display`, so `map_err` is only there for readability and could be removed with no change in behavior.

questions.explanation: The `?` operator needs the error type to be convertible via `From` into the function's error type, and with a plain `String` return type there is no `From` impl for most error types. Using `map_err` to turn the error into a `String` first makes the types match explicitly, whereas assuming `?` stringifies any error is the tempting misconception.
